body:
The theory of plate tectonics

The theory of plate tectonics explains the movement and interaction of the rigid plates that form the Earth's lithosphere. Developed into a unified scientific theory during the 1960s, it incorporates evidence from continental drift, sea-floor spreading, seismic activity and geological studies.

A tectonic plate consists of the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle. A plate may contain continental lithosphere, oceanic lithosphere or both.

The margins of tectonic plates are called plate boundaries. Most major tectonic activity is concentrated along these boundaries because neighbouring plates move relative to one another.

Major and smaller tectonic plates

A conventional school-level classification recognises the following 7 major plates:

  • Pacific Plate
  • North American Plate
  • South American Plate
  • Eurasian Plate
  • African Plate
  • Antarctic Plate
  • Indo-Australian Plate

Important smaller plates include the Nazca Plate, Cocos Plate, Caribbean Plate, Arabian Plate and Philippine Sea Plate.

The number of plates is not an absolute fixed geographical constant. Modern classifications may treat the Indian and Australian plates separately because they exhibit partly independent motion. Other large plates can also be subdivided.

Important geographical associations include the Nazca Plate west of South America, the Cocos Plate off Central America and the Philippine Sea Plate in the western Pacific region.

Classification of plate boundaries

Plate boundaries are classified according to the relative direction of movement between adjacent plates.

BoundaryRelative movementCrustal effectExample
DivergentAway from each otherCreation of new crustMid-Atlantic Ridge
ConvergentTowards each otherSubduction or crustal thickeningAndes, Himalayas
TransformHorizontally past each otherNeither systematically created nor consumedSan Andreas Fault

Divergent boundaries

At a divergent boundary, two plates move apart. This produces tensional forces that stretch and fracture the lithosphere.

When divergence occurs within a continent, the continental crust may become thinner and develop faults. Blocks of land may sink between faults, producing a rift valley. The East African Rift is a prominent example.

If continental separation continues sufficiently, a new ocean basin may form. Magma generated by decompression melting can produce new oceanic crust along a developing spreading centre.

The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is an example of oceanic divergence. It separates the North American Plate from the Eurasian Plate in the northern Atlantic and the South American Plate from the African Plate in the southern Atlantic.

Iceland lies across the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and is also influenced by a volcanic hotspot.

Convergent boundaries

At a convergent boundary, plates approach one another. The resulting compression may produce subduction, crustal thickening, uplift or mountain building, depending on the nature of the interacting plates.

Where dense oceanic lithosphere descends beneath another plate, the boundary is commonly called a destructive boundary because oceanic lithosphere is consumed. Continental collision, however, can lead primarily to shortening and thickening rather than extensive consumption of buoyant continental crust.

Transform boundaries

At transform boundaries, two plates move horizontally past one another. Their movement generates shear stress along faults.

Transform boundaries neither systematically produce new oceanic crust nor consume existing lithosphere. They are therefore also called conservative boundaries.

The San Andreas Fault in California is a major transform boundary between the Pacific and North American plates.

Transform faults frequently produce shallow earthquakes but are not normally associated with extensive magma generation. Many transform faults also connect offset segments of mid-oceanic ridges.

Prelims focus

  • A tectonic plate consists of lithosphere, not just crust.
  • Divergent boundaries are constructive boundaries.
  • Subduction commonly occurs at convergent boundaries.
  • Transform boundaries are conservative and involve horizontal sliding.
  • The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift and San Andreas Fault represent important boundary examples.
  • Trap: The Himalayas are a convergent collision zone, not an example of divergent or transform movement.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapter 4, pp. 31–34; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19, Chapter 3, pp. 12–13; USGS, This Dynamic Earth, Understanding Plate Motions; USGS, Are the Tectonic Plates Floating on Magma? Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Plate Tectonics, Major Plates and Types of Plate Boundaries

body:
Convergence and its geological consequences

When tectonic plates move towards one another, their lithosphere undergoes compression. The resulting landforms and geological activity depend largely on the density and buoyancy of the interacting plates.

Three basic combinations of convergence are recognised: oceanic-continental, oceanic-oceanic and continental-continental.

Oceanic-continental convergence

When oceanic lithosphere converges with continental lithosphere, the denser oceanic plate generally descends beneath the more buoyant continental plate. This process is called subduction.

As the oceanic plate bends downwards, it can form an oceanic trench near the boundary. Water released from minerals in the descending slab helps lower the melting temperature of the overlying mantle, allowing magma to form.

The magma may rise through the overriding continental crust, producing a chain of volcanoes. Compression and crustal deformation can simultaneously uplift a mountain range.

The Andes Mountains of South America provide a major example. The oceanic Nazca Plate descends beneath the South American Plate, forming the Peru-Chile Trench and contributing to mountain building, earthquakes and volcanism along western South America.

Oceanic-oceanic convergence

When 2 oceanic plates converge, one generally subducts beneath the other. The older, colder and denser plate often descends, although local tectonic conditions also influence which plate subducts.

This process can produce a deep oceanic trench and a curved chain of volcanic islands called an island arc.

The Mariana Trench and Mariana volcanic island arc in the western Pacific illustrate oceanic-oceanic subduction. The Pacific Plate descends beneath the Mariana Plate.

Continental-continental convergence

Continental crust is relatively buoyant and resists deep subduction compared with oceanic lithosphere. When 2 continental landmasses collide after an intervening ocean has largely closed, their crust is compressed, shortened and thickened.

Folding, thrust faulting and uplift produce extensive mountain systems and elevated plateaus. Powerful earthquakes can occur because compression and fault movement continue within the collision zone.

The Himalayas are the principal example of this type of convergence.

Formation of the Himalayas

India was originally part of Gondwanaland. After the breakup of the southern supercontinent, the Indian landmass moved northwards towards Eurasia.

The Tethys Ocean lay between the Indian and Eurasian landmasses. As India moved northwards, the intervening oceanic lithosphere was progressively consumed.

Continental collision approximately 40–50 million years ago, in the conventional school-level account, contributed to the formation of the Himalayas. The precise timing of the initial collision is a subject of geological research.

Compression folded and thrust sedimentary and other rocks, thickened the crust and produced extensive uplift. The Tibetan Plateau developed in association with this prolonged continental convergence and crustal thickening.

Convergence continues, making the Himalayan region tectonically active and susceptible to earthquakes.

Himalayas and Andes

The Himalayas represent continental-continental collision, while the Andes represent oceanic-continental subduction. Both are associated with compression and mountain building, but extensive subduction-related volcanic chains are characteristic of the Andes rather than the Himalayas.

Basic types of mountains

Fold mountains

Fold mountains develop when compressional forces deform rock layers, commonly producing folds, thrust faults, crustal thickening and uplift. The Himalayas and Alps are young fold mountain systems. The Aravalli Range, extending into Gujarat, represents an ancient and heavily eroded mountain system.

Block mountains and rift valleys

Faulting can displace large blocks of the Earth's crust vertically relative to adjacent blocks. A relatively elevated block between faults is called a horst, while a relatively lowered block is called a graben. The Rhine Rift Valley and the adjoining Vosges Mountains in Europe illustrate this relationship.

Volcanic mountains

Volcanic mountains form through the accumulation of lava, ash and other volcanic materials around eruptive openings. Their formation does not require the folding of pre-existing rock layers.

Prelims focus

  • Oceanic-continental convergence: trench, continental volcanic arc and mountain building.
  • Oceanic-oceanic convergence: trench and volcanic island arc.
  • Continental-continental convergence: crustal thickening and major mountain systems.
  • The Andes are associated with the Nazca and South American plates.
  • The Himalayas formed through Indian-Eurasian convergence following the closure of the Tethys Ocean.
  • Horst is a relatively raised fault block; graben is a relatively lowered fault block.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapter 4, pp. 33–34; NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 6, pp. 39–43; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, 2020 reprint, Chapters 5 and 7; USGS, This Dynamic Earth, Understanding Plate Motions and The Himalayas. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Subduction, Continental Collision and Mountain Building

body:
Origin of earthquakes

An earthquake is the shaking of the ground caused by the sudden release of energy within the Earth. Most earthquakes result from the movement of rocks along geological faults.

A fault is a fracture or zone of fractures in rock along which displacement has occurred. Tectonic movement generates stress within the surrounding rocks. Friction may prevent immediate movement along a fault, causing strain energy to accumulate.

When the accumulated stress overcomes the resistance to movement, the rocks slip suddenly and release energy in the form of seismic waves. This basic explanation is known as elastic rebound.

Focus and epicentre

  • Focus or hypocentre: The point within the Earth where earthquake rupture begins.
  • Epicentre: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.
  • Focal depth: The depth of the focus below the Earth's surface.

The epicentre identifies the surface position of an earthquake source. It is not necessarily the place that experiences the greatest damage because geological conditions, distance from the ruptured fault and the vulnerability of buildings also influence shaking and its effects.

Earthquake classification by depth

CategoryFocal depth
Shallow-focus0–70 km
Intermediate-focus70–300 km
Deep-focus300–700 km

These are conventional approximate depth categories. Most earthquakes originate at relatively shallow depths. Intermediate and deep earthquakes are characteristic of descending slabs in subduction zones.

Shallow earthquakes can be particularly damaging because their seismic energy travels a shorter distance before reaching the surface, although damage also depends on magnitude, local geology and construction quality.

Earthquake causes and tectonic settings

  • Tectonic earthquakes: Result from fault movement caused by geological stress. They form the principal category of earthquakes.
  • Volcanic earthquakes: Associated with magma movement and pressure changes in volcanic regions.
  • Collapse earthquakes: Small tremors resulting from the collapse of underground cavities or mines.
  • Reservoir-induced earthquakes: May occur when reservoir loading and changes in underground water pressure influence existing faults.

Divergent and transform boundaries are characterised mainly by shallow earthquakes. Subduction zones can generate shallow, intermediate and deep earthquakes. Continental collision zones can generate powerful earthquakes through compression and fault movement.

Magnitude and intensity

FeatureMagnitudeIntensity
MeaningSize of earthquake at its sourceSeverity of shaking and effects at a location
Common scalesRichter, Moment MagnitudeModified Mercalli
Spatial variationNot location-dependentVaries between locations
BasisSeismic measurementsObserved or estimated local effects

The Richter scale is a logarithmic magnitude scale originally developed for certain local earthquakes. The Moment Magnitude scale (Mw) is widely used for evaluating large earthquakes because it better represents the overall size of the rupture.

An increase of 1 magnitude unit corresponds approximately to 32 times more released seismic energy. On the original Richter amplitude scale, it represents a tenfold increase in measured wave amplitude after accounting for distance.

The Modified Mercalli scale has 12 conventional intensity levels, ranging from imperceptible shaking to catastrophic effects. One earthquake can produce different intensity values at different locations.

Earthquakes and tsunamis

A tsunami is a series of long waves generated by a sudden displacement of a large volume of water. Strong undersea earthquakes can produce tsunamis when fault movement significantly raises or lowers the ocean floor.

Not every undersea earthquake generates a tsunami. Its ability to do so depends particularly on the nature of fault displacement, the location of rupture and the amount of water displaced.

Other effects of earthquakes include ground displacement, landslides, structural collapse and soil liquefaction. Liquefaction occurs when loose, water-saturated sediments temporarily lose much of their strength during strong shaking.

Gujarat: The Kachchh earthquake region

Gujarat contains geologically significant fault systems, particularly within the Kachchh region. Kachchh has an ancient rift-related geological structure containing faults that can be reactivated by regional tectonic stress.

On 26 January 2001, the Bhuj earthquake occurred in Kachchh district. Its moment magnitude was approximately 7.7 according to USGS research.

The earthquake is an important example of an intraplate earthquake, occurring within a tectonic plate rather than directly along its principal boundary.

Although Gujarat is situated away from the main Himalayan collision boundary, tectonic stress can be transmitted through the Indian Plate and reactivate older faults in its interior.

Plate interiors are not necessarily earthquake-free

Most earthquakes are concentrated near plate boundaries, but significant earthquakes can also occur within plates. The 2001 Bhuj earthquake demonstrates this distinction.

Prelims focus

  • Focus is the underground rupture-initiation point; epicentre lies directly above it.
  • Intermediate and deep earthquakes are associated particularly with descending slabs.
  • Richter and Moment Magnitude measure earthquake size; Mercalli measures local intensity.
  • An increase of 1 magnitude unit represents approximately 32 times more released seismic energy.
  • The Bhuj earthquake occurred on 26 January 2001 and had an approximate moment magnitude of 7.7.
  • Trap: Neither all earthquakes nor all large earthquakes are restricted to plate boundaries.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19, Chapter 3, pp. 12–14; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapter 3, pp. 19–22; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 4; USGS, Determining the Depth of an Earthquake; USGS, Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity; Schweig and others, The Mw 7.7 Bhuj Earthquake: Global Lessons for Earthquake Hazard in Intra-Plate Regions, Journal of the Geological Society of India, 2003. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
